title: Defacement: Internal Defacement
summary: Internal defacement targets content that only the organisation can see: intranet pages, internal portals, server login banners, and the desktop background on user workstations. The purpose is intimidation and doubt rather than public messaging, because the audience is staff who already believe the network is protected. Typical mechanics are replacing a web page inside the corporate network, editing the text shown on a logon screen, or changing the wallpaper setting through the registry or a policy so the image appears for every user. Since the attacker already holds enough access to change appearance, this behaviour usually appears after the main intrusion goals have been met, which makes it a late but reliable signal. Evidence combines file integrity alerts in web roots with registry changes to desktop settings and the process tree that changed them.

beginner.definition: This is defacement aimed at people inside the company rather than the public. An attacker changes an internal web page, a login message, or a computer desktop picture. The message is seen only by staff. This sub-technique is the internal side of the wider defacement technique, which you should learn first.
beginner.whyItMatters: Staff who see strange messages on their own screens stop trusting the network. That fear can push people to make rushed decisions or to follow instructions they should ignore. Changing a login banner can also trick users into typing passwords into a fake prompt. Because these changes need deep access, they often show the attacker is already well established. Noticing them early can reveal a serious intrusion.
howItWorks: The attacker already has access to internal servers or to many user computers.
They find the internal page, logon message, or desktop setting that users see.
They replace the text or image with their own message or a disturbing picture.
For desktops, they change a stored setting so the new picture loads for that user or machine.
The change spreads through normal refresh, so many staff see it at the same time.
It is usually done late, after the attacker has finished the main goal.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital night desk where the screens behind reception show a welcome message to staff. An intruder who is already inside changes it to a threatening line. No patient records were touched and no medicine was taken. Yet every nurse walking past now feels that the building is not safe, and that feeling changes how they work for the rest of the shift.
takeaways: Internal defacement usually means the attacker has been inside for a while.
Watch for changes to internal web pages, logon banners and desktop settings.
Because it is meant to be seen, internal defacement is often a chance to catch the attacker.

objectives: Explain what internal defacement is and why an attacker would use it.
State how this sub-technique differs from the wider defacement technique.
Describe the internal content types that are commonly targeted.
Identify the telemetry that reveals a changed desktop setting or login banner.
Explain why internal defacement often happens late in an intrusion.
Describe how a changed login message could be used to mislead users.
